segments.voice: Yesterday, the Garuda, and its frame: Garuda asks, Vishnu answers, and readers differ on how to hear it. Today, the first of the after-death passages.

A kitchen on a quiet morning. Rice cooling on a steel plate. Black sesame in a small bowl, a cup of water beside it. Someone's grandmother wets her palms and presses the rice into small, firm balls, one after another, and sets them in a row. Nobody is going to eat them. In the days after a death, families who keep the old rites make offerings like this for the one who has gone. The Garuda Purana gives a reason for them, and it may not be the reason anyone guesses.
screen: `RICE ON A STEEL PLATE.` → `PRESSED INTO SMALL BALLS.` → `NOBODY WILL EAT THEM.`

segments.voice: In the Garuda Purana's account, a person who has just died isn't on their way yet. They're a preta, a departed one, in between, without a body to travel in. In paraphrase, Vishnu tells Garuda that the rice-ball offerings made in the days after death build that body, piece by piece, day by day, until the departed has a form that can make the journey. Then the long road begins. So in this picture the family isn't only grieving. They're doing something for the person they've lost: feeding them, in the text's terms, and getting them ready to go. The rice ball is called a pinda, and it comes back in later rites too, when the departed is joined to the ancestors and remembered year after year. Here the framing matters. Some families keep the rites as the text describes them, with a priest, on the set days. Some keep a few. Some hear the passage as a picture of something no one can see: that the dead are still owed care, and that grief can be given work to do. The text is clear about one thing. It puts the living and the dead in the same story, with the living doing their part. That's the first passage: a family making a body out of rice, so someone they love can travel.
screen: `A PRETA: IN BETWEEN.` · `THE PINDA BUILDS A BODY.` · `GRIEF GIVEN WORK TO DO.` · then, large: `THE LIVING HAVE A PART.`

segments.voice: With any pen and scrap of paper, write the name of someone you've lost, or someone far away, slowly, one letter at a time. Then rest your hand on the page and breathe with the name there. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
The Garuda. A Purana where Vishnu tells his eagle what the living can do for the dead, starting with a ball of rice.

howItsDone: In the days after a death, and at yearly remembrance rites (shraddha), Hindu families who keep these rites offer pindas, rice balls often mixed with sesame, usually with a priest's help; practice varies widely by family and region.

fork.setup: a classmate's grandmother died last week. her family offers rice each day, and she wonders why every day instead of once. by the Garuda Purana, why?

fork.reveal: in Vishnu's answer to Garuda, the offerings form the preta's body piece by piece, until it can make the journey.
